hook.question: I'm thinking of a number from 1 to 100. You can ask yes/no questions like "Is it more than 50?". How few questions do you need to be sure of my number?
paragraphs: The slow way is to ask "Is it 1? Is it 2? Is it 3?" and keep going. If I picked 100, that takes 100 questions.
Now ask "Is it more than 50?" and hear "yes". One question just crossed out 1 through 50. You never have to think about them again.
hook.aha: Each question halves what's left: 100 → 50 → 25 → 13 → 7 → 4 → 2 → 1. Seven questions are always enough, because that is how many times 100 can be halved. This is log₂: a million numbers take only 20 questions.

metaphor: To find "monkey" in a paper dictionary you don't start at page one. You open it in the middle and land on "M", then see that "monkey" comes later, so the whole front half of the book is out.
Open the middle of what's left, and again, and again. Each peek removes half of the pages, which is why even a huge dictionary takes only a few peeks.
mentalModel.click: Look at the middle. Because the list is sorted, that one look tells you which half can't hold your target, so throw that half away.

glossary.definition: The numbers go from smallest to largest, left to right. Binary search only works when this is true.
The left edge of the range where the target could still be.
The right edge of that range. Everything outside lo and hi has been ruled out.
The index in the middle of lo and hi. It is the one cell you look at each round.
The promise that stays true every round: if the target is in the array, it is somewhere between lo and hi.
The first position whose value is at least the target. It is also where the target would be inserted to keep the list sorted.
A yes/no answer that flips only once, like no, no, no, yes, yes, yes. That single flip is what lets you search for it by halving.

mentalModel.definition: Binary search finds a value, or the boundary where a yes/no answer flips, in a sorted or monotonic sequence. It keeps a range [lo, hi] that must contain the answer, looks at the middle element, and uses that one comparison to discard half of the range. The range shrinks from n to n/2 to n/4 and so on, so the search takes O(log n) comparisons and O(1) extra space.

useWhen: The data is sorted (or you can sort it once) and you need to find a value, or the spot where it belongs.
The problem asks for the minimum or maximum value that works: the smallest speed, the least capacity, the largest size.
You can test one candidate answer quickly, and the test is monotonic: if 5 works, then 6, 7 and 8 work too.
The statement asks for O(log n), or n is so big that looking at everything is too slow.
notWhen: The data is unsorted and you only need one lookup: a plain scan (or a hash map for many lookups) costs less than sorting first.
The yes/no test flips more than once: if 5 works, 6 fails and 7 works, one peek can't tell you which half to drop.
The data is in a linked list: you can't jump to the middle in one step, so every halving costs a walk.

quiz.problem: Given a sorted array of distinct integers and a target, return the index of the target, or -1 if it isn't there. It must run in O(log n).
quiz.explanation: Sorted data plus an O(log n) requirement is the textbook signal. Compare with the middle and drop half of the array each time.

quiz.problem: Koko has n piles of bananas and h hours. Each hour she eats from one pile at speed k. Find the smallest k that lets her finish all the piles in h hours.
quiz.explanation: Nothing is sorted, but the test "does speed k finish in time?" flips once: slow speeds fail, fast speeds pass. Binary search on the answer finds the first speed that passes.

quiz.problem: Given an unsorted array, return the indices of the two numbers that add up to a target.
quiz.explanation: The array is unsorted and you need many lookups. Storing each number you've seen in a hash map answers "have I seen target − x?" in one step.

quiz.problem: Given a sorted array, find two numbers anywhere in it that add up to a target.
quiz.explanation: You're not looking for one value, you're looking for a pair. One pointer at each end closes in on the answer, and each step rules out a whole end.

quiz.problem: Versions 1 to n of a product were shipped, and every version after the first bad one is also bad. Find the first bad version with as few checks as possible.
quiz.explanation: The checks read good, good, good, bad, bad, bad. A single flip is monotonic, so halving finds the boundary in O(log n) checks.

notes: Each round throws away half of the range, so n numbers need at most about log₂ n rounds. 1,000 numbers take 10 looks and a million take 20.
Write the middle as lo + (hi − lo) / 2. The shorter (lo + hi) / 2 can overflow a 32-bit int in Java and C++ when both are large. Both forms give the same answer otherwise.
Off-by-one bugs live in two places: the loop test and the moves. With an inclusive range [lo, hi] the loop is lo <= hi and the moves are mid + 1 and mid − 1, because mid has already been checked.

To find a boundary instead of a value (first position ≥ target, smallest speed that works), use the half-open range [lo, hi): loop while lo < hi, set hi = mid when mid might be the answer and lo = mid + 1 when it can't.
The array has to be sorted first. If it isn't, sorting costs O(n log n), which only pays off when you search many times.

examples.title: Binary Search
examples.problem: Given a sorted array of integers nums and an integer target, return the index of target in nums, or -1 if it is not there. Your solution must run in O(log n).
approach: The array is sorted, so one comparison with the middle can rule out half of it.
lo = 0, hi = 5, so mid = 2 and nums[2] = 3. That is smaller than 9, so drop the left half: lo = 3.
Now lo = 3, hi = 5, so mid = 4 and nums[4] = 9. That is the target, so return 4.
If lo ever passes hi, every position has been ruled out, so return -1.

examples.title: Search Insert Position
examples.problem: Given a sorted array of distinct integers and a target, return the index of the target if it is found. If not, return the index where it would be inserted to keep the array sorted. Run in O(log n).
approach: The insert position is the first index whose number is at least the target. That is the "first position ≥ target" template.
Search the half-open range [0, 4). mid = 2 holds 5, which is at least 2, so mid might be the answer: hi = 2.
mid = 1 holds 3, at least 2 again, so hi = 1. mid = 0 holds 1, below 2, so skip it: lo = 1.
lo and hi meet at 1, so 2 belongs at index 1. If every number were smaller, lo would end at n, one past the end.

examples.title: Koko Eating Bananas
examples.problem: Koko has piles of bananas and h hours. Each hour she picks one pile and eats k bananas from it (finishing early if the pile has fewer, but not moving on until the hour is up). Return the smallest k that lets her eat all the piles within h hours.
approach: Nothing here is sorted, but the speeds are: if speed k is fast enough, so is every speed above it. The test flips from "too slow" to "fast enough" exactly once.
Search the speeds 1 to 11 (the biggest pile) for the first one that works. At speed k a pile takes ceil(pile / k) hours, so add those up.
k = 6 takes 1 + 1 + 2 + 2 = 6 hours, which fits in 8, so keep it. k = 3 takes 10 hours, too slow. k = 5 takes 8, fits.
k = 4 also takes 1 + 2 + 2 + 3 = 8 hours, and lo = hi = 4, so the smallest working speed is 4. It is the same first-true loop, with an hours calculation as the test.
examples.time: O(n log m), where m is the biggest pile

conceptQuiz.question: You compare nums[mid] with the target in a sorted array and nums[mid] is smaller. What now?
options: Search only the right half, starting at mid + 1.
Stop: the target isn't in the array.
conceptQuiz.explanation: The array is sorted, so everything left of mid is even smaller than nums[mid]. The target can only be to the right, and mid itself has already been checked.

conceptQuiz.question: About how many looks does binary search need, at most, to search 1,000 sorted numbers?
conceptQuiz.explanation: Each look halves the range: 1,000 → 500 → 250 and so on. 2 multiplied by itself 10 times is 1,024, so 10 looks are enough.

conceptQuiz.question: Why write mid = lo + (hi − lo) / 2 instead of (lo + hi) / 2?
options: lo + hi can overflow an int when both are large; this form never does.
It is much faster to compute.
It makes mid round up instead of down.
It lets the method work on unsorted arrays.
conceptQuiz.explanation: hi − lo is never bigger than hi, so adding it to lo stays in range. Adding lo + hi first can pass the largest int in Java or C++.

conceptQuiz.question: In the "first position ≥ target" loop, why is it hi = mid and not hi = mid − 1 when nums[mid] ≥ target?
options: Because mid itself might be the first big-enough number.
Because the loop would never stop otherwise.
conceptQuiz.explanation: nums[mid] is big enough, but something to its left might be too. Dropping mid could throw away the very answer you are looking for, so you keep it as the new edge.

conceptQuiz.question: Which of these is a good fit for "binary search on the answer"?
options: Find the largest number in an unsorted list.
Find the smallest ship capacity that delivers every package within D days, when a bigger ship never hurts.
Count the vowels in a word.
conceptQuiz.explanation: Capacity is monotonic: if a ship can do the job, any bigger ship can too. You can test one capacity quickly, so you halve the range of capacities.

practice.title: First Bad Version
practice.insight: The checks read good, good, bad, bad: the first-true shape. Keep mid when it is bad, because it could be the first one.

practice.title: Sqrt(x)
practice.insight: You are searching the numbers 0 to x for the biggest m with m * m <= x. Compare with m <= x / m to dodge overflow.

practice.title: Find First and Last Position of Element in Sorted Array
practice.insight: Run the first-position search twice: once for the first index with a value ≥ target, once for the first index with a value > target.

practice.title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array
practice.insight: Compare nums[mid] with the last element. That one comparison tells you whether the drop (the minimum) is on the left or the right of mid.

practice.title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
practice.insight: At any mid, at least one half is still properly sorted. Check whether the target falls inside that sorted half, and keep that half or drop it.

practice.title: Capacity To Ship Packages Within D Days
practice.insight: Binary search on the answer: try a capacity, simulate loading the days, and ask whether it fits. The smallest capacity can't be less than the heaviest package.

practice.title: Search a 2D Matrix
practice.insight: If you read the rows one after another the matrix is one sorted list. Turn a middle index into a row and column with division and remainder.

practice.title: Median of Two Sorted Arrays
practice.insight: Don't merge. Binary search how many elements the shorter array gives to the left half, until both left-side maxima are at most both right-side minima.

overview: Explain why halving the range takes only about log₂ n steps.
Trace lo, hi and mid through a sorted array until you find the target.
Spot "minimum value that works" questions that can be binary searched.
Choose between closed [lo, hi] and half-open [lo, hi) boundary loops.
Avoid the midpoint overflow bug by writing lo + (hi - lo) / 2.
